item.title: CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
item.description:
CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

  • CVE-2026-133968 Project MONAI MONAI Label Path Traversal Vulnerability

  •  CVE-2026-134624 N-able Mail Assure (SpamExperts) Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

This vulnerability will be addressed in an upcoming Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series software release (version 5.5.x). In addition, Danfoss will remove the ability for users to disable Strict Mode in future software releases.

Until a software update is available, Danfoss recommends the following mitigations: * Follow the guidance provided in the product documentation and do not expose devices directly to the Internet or assign them public IP addresses. * Restrict remote access to affected devices by using a secure VPN or other protected network architecture. * Configure all affected devices to operate in Strict Mode, which provides enhanced security protections. * Use strong, unique passwords for all user accounts and administrative access. * For additional security recommendations and best practices see the Danfoss AK-SM 800 security guidance page: https://www.danfoss.com/en/service-and-support/downloads/dcs/adap-kool-software/ak-sm-800a/#tab-overview

Apply these controls as appropriate based on the vulnerability, assessed risk, operational requirements, and characteristics of your environment. Implement changes under your established management-of-change process. Before implementing isolation, access-control, or network-configuration changes, evaluate potential impacts to safety, availability, and essential operational functions. • Isolate affected engineering workstations and OT systems from external and nonessential networks, including the internet and corporate IT networks, where operationally feasible. • Disable or tightly restrict vendor, contractor, and other remote access to the affected OT environment until the vulnerability can be remediated. Where practicable and appropriate to the assessed risk, use dedicated or physically separated infrastructure for higher-criticality systems. Where logical segmentation is used, ensure segmentation controls are appropriately configured, secured, and monitored. • Restrict both physical and logical access to affected systems to authorized personnel only. Apply least-privilege principles to administrative, engineering, maintenance, and service access. • Configure application allowlisting, where supported, so that only trusted and pre-approved applications are permitted to execute. Block unauthorized software. • Use appropriate antivirus or endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools where supported and compatible with the affected system. Configure host-based and network firewalls to permit only required communications. • Disable unnecessary services, ports, protocols, and communication pathways associated with the affected systems. Where a service or protocol cannot be disabled for operational reasons, restrict access to trusted systems and authorized users wherever possible. • Enable and regularly review available system, security, and network logs to identify suspicious or unauthorized activity. Where appropriate, monitor communications to and from affected systems for unexpected connections or changes in network behavior. • Maintain secure, tested, and preferably offline backups of PLC programs, device configurations, engineering workstation configurations, and other information necessary to restore operations. Periodically verify that backups can be successfully restored. • Verify that critical OT functions can continue operating without unnecessary dependencies on external networks, cloud services, remote-access services, corporate IT services, or other nonessential systems. • If removable media is required to transfer files into an isolated or restricted environment, use controlled and trusted media and scan it for malicious content before use. • Continuously evaluate the risks associated with operating vulnerable or outdated firmware or software. How DARPA Challenged Teams to Bring Robots Into Disaster Triage
item.description:
On 5 November, 10 teams descended upon a 52-acre mock town in College Station, Texas called Disaster City. They were there for a nine-day competition to see how well teams of robots and humans could navigate simulated catastrophes, like a market ravaged by a tornado and a nighttime strike on a military base. At stake? US $2.5 million in prize money.

The scenarios were the final of the DARPA Triage Challenge, which the U.S. agency has been running for three years with the goal of saving more lives in urgent mass casualty events. Engineers from academia and industry have competed in elaborately staged mass casualty events, such as simulated combat zones and plane crash scenes. Teams spent years designing systems where autonomous ground robots and drones could help first responders find mock victims and decide the best way to care for them. “Triage is all about resources,” says Jeremy Pamplin, who managed the challenge for DARPA. Pamplin is a critical care physician and retired colonel who spent 28 years in the U.S. Army.

In mass casualty events, medics race to assess trauma with finite resources and limited time. Some victims need urgent help that medics can provide immediately, like tourniquets to halt bleeding. Some need evacuation and surgery. Others don’t need immediate help—either because their wounds are minimal enough, or because they’re so severe that a medic’s attention is better served elsewhere. Medics must prioritize who gets what care, but the line between each of these scenarios can be murky amid the rubble, frenzy, and heat of the moment.

It’s a difficult problem, and so the technologies developed in this competition could help real-world decisionmaking, says Gabriela Garcia Dolagaray, assistant medical director for emergency preparedness at Massachusetts General Hospital and the Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Boston. “Finding people can sometimes just be dangerous,” she says, “and getting a robust number of people to go out and search in a disaster area will take time.”

Trauma Technologies and the DARPA Triage Challenge

The Triage Challenge is the latest in a long DARPA legacy of running grand challenges to incentivize proof-of-concept development of important technologies. This particular challenge began as a program to quickly detect signs of trauma. DARPA imagined not only that drones and robots could find casualties, but that machine learning algorithms could assist in triage—which, at its core, is the process of assessing injuries and prioritizing care in a medical emergency.

Pamplin took over the competition in May 2025. “I have friends that still wake up in the middle of the night with these types of recollections and wondering if they did the right thing in the moment during a mass casualty incident,” Pamplin says. “That moves me. I would very much like to eliminate that uncertainty for them to the extent possible with this type of technology.”

He used his experience to make the competition increasingly elaborate and realistic. Year one featured a simulated convoy attack, and human participants sat in protective enclosures to avoid incidental run-ins with robots. In year two, when Pamplin took over the challenge, his team incorporated a full-size airplane fuselage to simulate a plane crash with dozens of victims. Organizers learned to recreate the physical environment of a disaster, and also the physical signs of injuries, like warm blood. Pamplin’s team visited a slaughterhouse with thermal cameras to study the temperature of blood spilling onto the ground. In the competition, they mimic that effect by heating water in a coffee pot and pouring it beside the body. This lets teams detect bleeding even at night.

A man performs a simulated triage as part of DARPA’s Triage Challenge finals. The program was designed to see how robots could assist in making triage decisions during an emergency.Paul Flacks/DARPA

“They always are throwing additional challenging things at us that you wouldn’t expect,” says Sam Colachis, a biomedical engineer at Battelle, an applied science and technology nonprofit in Columbus Ohio who led the organization’s DART team—short for “Drone-Assisted Rapid Triage”—in the competition.

The tactics required for successful triage are inherently multidisciplinary, says Derek Paley, a professor of aerospace engineering leading the University of Maryland’s team, RoboScout. Before 2022, Paley felt confident in his lab’s skills with autonomous navigation and algorithms, but he knew little about trauma medicine. “I didn’t even know what triage was,” he says.

Paley recruited colleagues in emergency medicine to help design his team’s approach and shape their tech. Before the Triage Challenge began, they felt like an underdog. “We kind of have a chip on our shoulder because we think we can play on the same field as these other teams…who’ve done grand challenges before,” Paley told Spectrum before the competition. They finished third in the first year of competition and second last year.

Each year’s competition began with four smaller trials that tested specific components of a robotic system. Teams first released their robots to locate as many casualties (a mix of live actors and manikins) as possible in 15 minutes. Next, they spent five minutes triaging injuries. Another trial presented teams with a fixed number of casualties in known locations to test how they assess trauma. Then, teams had ten minutes to collect vitals like pulse and breathing rate remotely from a few meters away. The top four teams moved into a semi-final where their robots worked with two human medics in simulated emergencies. And the two teams who performed best in four human-machine runs then moved to a 25-minute championship run.

Robots, Drones, and Autonomous Triage

When the teams arrived at Disaster City, they knew very little about the details of what awaited them. One self-funded team of college students from Delhi Technological University flew from India with 22 checked bags, each containing disembodied drones and wheeled robots they had handbuilt. Their team, Unmanned Aerial Systems, learned in the two prior years of the contest to simply expect the unexpected—from DARPA and their own systems. Upon arrival this year, they unzipped their luggage to find broken motors and chassis, camera parts, and missing screws. “We’re still trying to assemble everything before the competition,” Nishant Chandna calmly told IEEE Spectrum a couple days before the challenge. “It’s just part of it.”

Most teams in the challenge designed systems with a mix of ground robots and aerial drones. The student team from India built drones and wheeled robots to search for mock victims with onboard cameras and lidar.

But wheeled robots are problematic. They are more stable, cheaper, and easier to control than legged robots, but they struggle with stairs, entryways, and rough terrain littered with rubble. “We really needed a platform that could traverse those obstacles pretty easily,” says Eric Eaton, a machine learning scientist who led the University of Pennsylvania’s team, which began with drones and wheeled robots before expanding their fleet with four-legged Spot robots from Boston Dynamics that make it up stairs.

Paley’s RoboScout team opted for a strategy that involved sensing the scene from the ground. Their “dogs,” which were also Spot robots, listen for screaming victims, and help in one of the most difficult challenges in autonomous triage: quickly sensing vitals from with thermal cameras and radar. Millimeter-wave radar can detect the subtle movement of a pulse, and thermal cameras can measure breathing rates based on how breathing changes the temperature around a mouth and nose.

Battelle’s team had relied entirely on drones, even for measuring vital signs. Colachis says his team fuses inputs from multiple sensors including thermal, radar, and visual to calculate vitals. The team became almost notorious for their commitment to drones. “They keep threatening to bring a ground robot,” says RoboScout’s Paley, “but they always show up with drones.” For the first two years of the competition, it worked—Battelle won the first two rounds of the competition.

Members of the University of Maryland’s RoboScout team (on right) celebrate a successful run during the DARPA Triage Challenge finals.Paul Flacks/DARPA

RoboScout Wins DARPA Triage Grand Prize

During the final, organizers cast more than 500 actors to simulate casualties throughout the week. DARPA chose these actors to make obstacles like sensing vitals more realistic than previous years. Some were college students instructed to increase their heart and breathing rate on exercise bikes to simulate shock. Endurance athletes were instructed to lower their heart rates, simulating other injuries like airway failures. In the military base simulation, soldiers were running around a compound with alarms blaring. “Some of the explosions caused some of the medics to actually react to it,” Pamplin says, and “pull people to the ground so they didn’t get hit.”

Battelle did finally show up with a ground robot to help with measuring vitals remotely. But this time, the twice-champ finished second. The winner of DARPA’s Triage Challenge grand prize was the RoboScout team from the University of Maryland. The grand prize earned them $1.5 million.

After a perilous start slowed by software errors relating to the competition’s timer and Wi-Fi RoboScout rallied back through the final human-machine teaming portion. “We got hot at the right time,” Paley says. “It was pretty surreal.”

Other teams performed well despite having to improvise through engineering hiccups. Carnegie Mellon’s team, Chiron, struggled with a GPS error. After fixing it, they raced back and nearly made the final. The student team from Delhi didn’t meet a threshold for autonomous control in the competition, but they did earn the highest score in one sub-competition, winning $300,000.

“It’s an incredibly exciting challenge,” says Peter Fischer, trauma medical director with Washington Regional Medical Center in Fayetteville, Arkansas. “We struggle, especially with mass casualty incidents, in determining who the sickest patients are. In trauma, especially, you have to make sure that you triage these patients appropriately, so the sickest ones not only get the care the fastest, but get to the right place at the right time.”

Fischer was intrigued by a non-robotic branch of the competition, where two new teams excelled in predicting urgent care with the help of AI agents. He imagines these advances in robotics and algorithms could connect with additional data from hospitals. Triage algorithms could suggest where to take them to avoid overloading specific hospitals, he says, “That’s where we can really start to make a big difference.”

Although the competition has ended, the work continues. Several participants told IEEE Spectrum they plan to bring their teams’ AI algorithms elsewhere, such as hospital trauma bays, regional medical emergencies, and chemical weapon response.

For his part, DARPA’s Pamplin was most eager to compare performance to human medics without robots. A human-only team located 50 percent of casualties on average in daytime simulations; when paired with medics on one run of the same course, Maryland’s robots found every one. “That was the first time we’ve ever seen that,” he says. In the championship run, humans provided life-saving interventions to 25 percent of the mock casualties who needed them—RoboScout treated 74 percent. “That’s a couple lives,” Pamplin says. “That’s a couple humans that didn’t die that day.”

1. Conflict background and armed actors

According to Amnesty International, Balochistan experienced increased military operations amid ongoing attacks by armed groups and heightened tensions between Pakistan and India in 2025, with militant violence, drone strikes and security operations resulting in ‘dozens’ of civilian deaths during the year. 1 More specifically, according to the South Asia Terrorism Portal (SATP), Balochistan recorded 1 244 ‘terrorism-related’ incidents between January and 9 November 2026, compared with 848 in 2025. 2 The same source noted that between January and 9 November 2026, militant-related violence and counterterrorism operations in Balochistan resulted in 2 596 deaths, including 446 civilians, 778 security personnel and 1 371 militants.

Throughout 2026, militant violence continued in Balochistan. 4 Al Jazeera identified political marginalisation, economic grievances and concerns over the distribution of benefits from the province's natural resources as underlying factors in the conflict. 5 It also reported that some Baloch groups viewed major development projects, including the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), as benefiting external interests while leaving local communities marginalised.

Concerning the Baloch separatist movement, Reuters reported that the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA), the largest of several separatist armed groups operating in the province, seeks independence for Balochistan.7 The group claims that the Pakistani government exploits Balochistan’s natural gas and mineral resources. 8 It has also carried out attacks against security forces, infrastructure and Chinese interests, 9 as well as disrupted electoral processes.

Information on the armed groups in the province can be found in section 4.2.1. Balochistan, subsection (b), Presence and general activities of the armed actors, of the EUAA COI report Pakistan, Country Focus, published in May 2026.

Additional information on the general security situation in Pakistan can be found in the EUAA COI query response number Q23-2026: Major political, human rights and security developments, published in July 2026.

item.title: Sudan: Más de 380 000 personas desplazadas en Kordofán, Sudán, mientras la violencia obliga a miles más a huir
item.description:
Country: Sudan
Source: International Organization for Migration

Jartum, 26 de noviembre de 2026 – Más de 383 000 personas fueron desplazadas de la región sudanesa de Kordofán entre octubre de 2025 y octubre de 2026, mientras que la renovada inseguridad obligó a otras 15 000 personas a huir solo en noviembre. La Organización Internacional para las Migraciones (OIM) advierte que las sucesivas oleadas de desplazamiento están agravando una crisis humanitaria ya crítica, dejando a miles de familias sin alojamiento seguro, acceso a servicios básicos ni medios de subsistencia.

"Las familias de todo Kordofán se ven obligadas a huir una y otra vez, mientras que las comunidades que las acogen ya tienen dificultades para satisfacer sus propias necesidades básicas", declaró Mohamed Refaat, Jefe de Misión de la OIM en Sudán. "Los civiles deben ser protegidos. A medida que más personas son expulsadas de sus hogares, necesitamos urgentemente los recursos y el acceso seguro para llegar a ellas antes de que su situación se deteriore aún más".

Kordofán Occidental ha sido especialmente afectado por la última oleada de desplazamiento. Solo en noviembre, la Matriz de Seguimiento del Desplazamiento (DTM) de la OIM registró 21 incidentes de desplazamiento en toda la región, que obligaron a aproximadamente 15 310 personas a abandonar sus hogares. Casi el 90 por ciento de estos desplazamientos se originaron en Kordofán Occidental, con alrededor de 12 720 personas obligadas a huir únicamente de la localidad de Abu Zabad.

Muchas familias se han visto obligadas a desplazarse en repetidas ocasiones, agotando sus ya limitados recursos e interrumpiendo el acceso a la atención sanitaria, la educación y otros servicios esenciales. El creciente número de personas que buscan refugio en Kordofán Septentrional, el Nilo Blanco y Jartum ejerce una presión adicional sobre las comunidades de acogida y unos servicios ya sobrecargados.

Las condiciones humanitarias son especialmente preocupantes en Kordofán Occidental, donde el 70 por ciento de los hogares encuestados en el marco de la Evaluación Multisectorial de Necesidades de la OIM de 2026 indicaron tener necesidades de protección, mientras que el acceso a la atención sanitaria y la educación seguía estando gravemente limitado. En todo Sudán, el 38 por ciento de los hogares encuestados indicaron tener necesidades de alojamiento no satisfechas. En Kordofán, el desplazamiento reiterado, los daños a las viviendas y la pérdida de pertenencias esenciales han dejado a muchas familias sin un alojamiento adecuado o seguro.

La OIM continúa realizando el seguimiento del desplazamiento en Kordofán y otras zonas afectadas de Sudán para identificar necesidades emergentes y orientar los esfuerzos de respuesta humanitaria. En colaboración con sus socios, la OIM contribuye a proporcionar asistencia humanitaria, incluido alojamiento de emergencia, artículos de socorro básicos y otros servicios esenciales.

Ante la inseguridad que sigue impulsando el desplazamiento en todo Kordofán, la OIM hace un llamamiento a la protección de la población civil y las infraestructuras civiles, al acceso humanitario seguro y sin obstáculos, y a la aportación urgente de financiación adicional para atender las necesidades crecientes. Sin un apoyo inmediato, miles de familias más corren el riesgo de quedarse sin la asistencia que necesitan para sobrevivir.

Notas para los editores

  • Durante noviembre de 2026, la OIM registró 21 incidentes de desplazamiento en toda la región de Kordofán, que afectaron a un estimado de 15 310 personas. Dieciséis de estos incidentes se registraron en Kordofán Occidental, donde aproximadamente 13 515 personas fueron desplazadas. Las cifras se basan en los informes de campo de la Matriz de Seguimiento del Desplazamiento (DTM) de la OIM.
  • Las necesidades humanitarias citadas en este comunicado provienen de la Evaluación Multisectorial de Necesidades de Sudán de 2026 (MSNA) de la OIM. La evaluación ofrece una visión más amplia de las necesidades humanitarias en Kordofán Occidental y no debe interpretarse como una evaluación de las 12 720 personas desplazadas recientemente en la localidad de Abu Zabad.
  • Puede consultarse información adicional sobre el desplazamiento reciente en la localidad de Abu Zabad a través de las Alertas Rápidas de la DTM de la OIM en Sudán: ciudad de Abu Zabad, aldea de Abu Galib y múltiples aldeas en la localidad de Abu Zabad.

Se alienta a los editores a utilizar material audiovisual reciente de la OIM procedente de Sudán para complementar su cobertura de la crisis, disponible para su visualización y descarga en UNifeed.

Para más información, visite el Centro de Prensa de la OIM.

item.title: Sudan: Plus de 380 000 personnes déplacées dans la région du Kordofan au Soudan alors que la violence pousse des milliers d'autres à fuir
item.description:
Country: Sudan
Source: International Organization for Migration

Khartoum, 26 novembre 2026 – Plus de 383 000 personnes ont été déplacées de la région du Kordofan au Soudan entre octobre 2025 et octobre 2026, une recrudescence de l'insécurité ayant contraint 15 000 personnes supplémentaires à fuir en novembre seulement. L'Organisation internationale pour les migrations (OIM) avertit que des vagues successives de déplacements aggravent une crise humanitaire déjà sévère, laissant des milliers de familles sans abri sûr, sans accès aux services de base ni aux moyens de subvenir à leurs besoins.

« Des familles à travers le Kordofan sont contraintes de fuir à maintes reprises, tandis que les communautés qui les accueillent peinent déjà à satisfaire leurs propres besoins essentiels », a déclaré Mohamed Refaat, Chef de mission de l'OIM au Soudan. « Les civils doivent être protégés. À mesure que davantage de personnes sont forcées de quitter leur foyer, nous avons urgemment besoin de ressources et d'un accès sécurisé pour les atteindre avant que leur situation ne se détériore encore davantage. »

Le Kordofan occidental a été particulièrement touché par la dernière vague de déplacement. En novembre seulement, la Matrice de suivi des déplacements (DTM) de l'OIM a enregistré 21 épisodes de déplacement dans la région, forçant environ 15 310 personnes à quitter leur foyer. Près de 90 % des personnes déplacées provenaient du Kordofan occidental, dont quelque 12 720 de la seule localité d'Abu Zabad.

De nombreuses familles ont été contraintes de se déplacer à plusieurs reprises, épuisant leurs ressources déjà limitées et perturbant leur accès aux soins de santé, à l'éducation et à d'autres services essentiels. Le nombre croissant de personnes cherchant refuge dans le Kordofan du Nord, le Nil Blanc et Khartoum exerce une pression supplémentaire sur les communautés hôtes et les services essentiels déjà sous pression.

Les conditions humanitaires sont particulièrement préoccupantes dans le Kordofan occidental, où 70 % des ménages interrogés dans le cadre de l'Évaluation multisectorielle des besoins 2026 de l'OIM ont signalé des besoins de protection, tandis que l'accès aux soins de santé et à l'éducation demeurait gravement limité. À travers le Soudan, 38 % des ménages interrogés ont signalé des besoins non satisfaits en matière d'abri. Dans le Kordofan, les déplacements répétés, les dommages causés aux habitations et la perte de biens essentiels ont privé de nombreuses familles d'un abri adéquat et sûr.

L'OIM continue de suivre les déplacements dans le Kordofan et d'autres zones affectées du Soudan afin d'identifier les besoins émergents et d'orienter les efforts de réponse humanitaire. En collaboration avec ses partenaires, l'OIM soutient les efforts visant à fournir une aide humanitaire d'urgence, notamment des abris d'urgence, des articles ménagers essentiels et d'autres services essentiels.

Alors que l'insécurité continue de provoquer des déplacements à travers le Kordofan, l'OIM appelle à la protection des civils et des infrastructures civiles, à un accès humanitaire sûr et sans entraves, ainsi qu'à la mobilisation urgente de financements supplémentaires pour répondre aux besoins croissants. En l'absence d'un soutien immédiat, des milliers de familles supplémentaires risquent de se retrouver sans l'assistance dont elles ont besoin pour survivre.

Notes à l'intention des rédacteurs

  • Au cours du mois de novembre 2026, l'OIM a enregistré 21 épisodes de déplacement dans la région du Kordofan, entraînant le déplacement d'environ 15 310 personnes. Seize de ces épisodes ont été enregistrés dans le Kordofan occidental, où environ 13 515 personnes ont été déplacées. Ces chiffres sont issus des rapports de terrain de la Matrice de suivi des déplacements (DTM) de l'OIM.
  • Les besoins humanitaires cités dans ce communiqué sont tirés de l'Évaluation multisectorielle des besoins au Soudan 2026 de l'OIM (MSNA). Cette évaluation offre une vue d'ensemble des besoins humanitaires dans le Kordofan occidental et ne doit pas être interprétée comme une évaluation des 12 720 personnes récemment déplacées dans la localité d'Abu Zabad.
  • Des informations complémentaires sur les déplacements récents dans la localité d'Abu Zabad sont disponibles via les Alertes rapides DTM Soudan de l'OIM : ville d'Abu Zabad, village d'Abu Galib et plusieurs villages dans la localité d'Abu Zabad.

Les rédacteurs sont invités à utiliser les récentes images de l'OIM en provenance du Soudan pour compléter leur couverture de la crise, disponibles en consultation et en téléchargement sur UNifeed.

Pour plus d'informations, veuillez consulter le Centre médias de l'OIM.

item.title: Update 377 – IAEA Director General Statement on Situation in Ukraine
item.description:
Country: Ukraine
Source: International Atomic Energy Agency

The IAEA is engaging with the Russian Federation and Ukraine on arrangements for a ninth localized ceasefire at the Zaporizhzhya Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) following another loss of offsite power.

The plant’s connection to its sole remaining external power line, the 330 kV Ferosplavna-1 line, was lost on 25 November at 05:28 local time, reportedly due to military activity. For the 28th time during the conflict, ZNPP is relying on emergency diesel generators for essential nuclear safety and security functions.

“Once again we are faced with a loss of offsite power at the ZNPP. Its continued reliance on a single power line, together with the plant’s location on the front line of an active warzone, results in an extremely precarious offsite power connection,” said IAEA Director General Rafael Mariano Grossi.

“I call on both sides to work constructively with the IAEA to cease military activity against electrical infrastructure, facilitate repair of the Ferosplavna-1 line and re-establish an offsite power connection to the ZNPP,” said Director General Grossi.

This event further underscores the importance of negotiations to facilitate repair of the Dniprovska 750 kV power line and its associated substation. The substation was reportedly damaged during military activity in May. The power line was repaired under the sixth Agency-negotiated temporary localized ceasefire in June, but further damage was subsequently identified. The Dniprovska substation and 750 kV line are essential components of the ZNPP's energy infrastructure.

Diesel fuel at the ZNPP

The four emergency diesel generators in automatic standby at the ZNPP, out of a total of 19 available emergency diesel generators, started automatically when power was lost. Two have since been shut down to conserve diesel fuel. To further conserve diesel fuel reserves during this period, the plant has suspended on-site heating, despite temperatures at the site falling to as low as 0°C this week.

The IAEA estimates that the ZNPP has sufficient diesel fuel to maintain its current configuration of two operating emergency diesel generators for more than ten days. The IAEA continues to closely monitor diesel fuel stocks and consumption at the ZNPP.

Over the past months, the Agency has received varying information regarding the availability and location of diesel fuel at the site and is seeking further clarification to independently assess the current diesel fuel situation.

To further optimize diesel fuel use while maintaining essential safety functions, the ZNPP has shut down all reactor heat removal pumps and is currently operating only the spent fuel pool cooling pumps on Units 1 and 6. Coolant temperatures remain within normal operational limits, but are rising, meaning that pumps will need to be periodically restarted to control temperatures within safe limits.

“The diesel fuel conservation measures help the plant deliver its fundamental safety functions. Yet the cold conditions and the decision to only operate safety related equipment periodically underline the challenges facing staff at the site,” said Director General Grossi.

Military activity

The IAEA team at the ZNPP reported hearing military activity every day throughout the week, while the ZNPP alleged that attacks occurred on civilian vehicles on site.

Elsewhere in Ukraine, other nuclear power plants (NPPs) continued to report fluctuations in power output due to grid instability linked to military activity, including the loss of multiple off-site power lines.

Over the past week, a total of 143 air raid alerts occurred. Drones were reported at three of the sites in Ukraine where IAEA staff are present: 10 at the Khmelnytskyy NPP, 26 at the South Ukraine NPP — one of which reportedly passed directly over the plant — and 91 at the Chornobyl NPP. Drones were also reported as close as 100 m to the Centralised Spent Fuel Storage Facility, which is located in the Chornobyl Exclusion Zone.

“I once again call for the end of military activity near all nuclear facilities. As I have said before: no one benefits from a nuclear disaster,” said Director General Grossi.

IAEA assistance to Ukraine

Also this week, under the IAEA’s assistance programme for Ukraine, dose rate meters and a hot water tank were delivered to the National Research Center for Radiation Medicine. Air handling units and air conditioners were provided to the Chornobyl NPP, while filtering polymeric fibrous material was delivered to the Ukrainian Hydrometeorological Center and related organizations of the State Emergency Service of Ukraine. These deliveries were made possible through funding provided by Japan.

Country: Libya
Source: UN Children's Fund

Libya Launches National Integrated Project to Reduce Violence Against Children.

Government-led project brings together families, schools, services and communities around a shared national approach to prevention and protection.

TRIPOLI, 26 November 2026 – The Government of Libya today launched the National Integrated Project for Reducing Violence Against Children, marking an important step towards strengthening prevention, protection and support for children across the country.

Led by the Ministry of Education, together with the Ministries of Social Affairs and Health, and with technical support from UNICEF, the initiative brings national institutions together around a common goal: helping children grow and learn in safe, supportive environments.

During the ceremony, H.E the Minister of Education, Mohamed Al-Qariou "Protecting children from violence is a national responsibility that begins with prevention." Through this project, we are uniting the efforts of families, schools and national institutions under a shared approach that places children's safety, dignity and well-being at the heart of our work. Our commitment is to turn these efforts into sustainable practices that guarantee every child a safe and supportive environment in which to learn and grow.

National evidence has reinforced the need for a more comprehensive and sustainable approach to prevent violence against children. Statistical findings published by the Ministry of Planning have highlighted concerning levels of violence, underscoring the importance of moving beyond responding after violence occurs towards earlier prevention and more positive practices within families, schools and communities.

“A child’s sense of safety is built in everyday moments; in how they are spoken to at home, how they are treated at school, and whether they know that someone will listen when they need help,” said Abdullahi Mohammed, UNICEF Representative in Libya. “By working together, we can turn that sense of safety into everyday reality. UNICEF remains committed to supporting national efforts to strengthen prevention, protection and care for every child in Libya.”

The development and preparation of the project have been supported through contributions from the European Union, the Kingdom of the Netherlands and GIZ, alongside UNICEF. This support has contributed to the technical development and adaptation of the programme, capacity building, and readiness for implementation.

Following the launch, the project will move into its next phase of nationwide implementation across 19 municipalities in Libya. Through a municipal-level cascade model, the project aims to build a future network of approximately 5,000 facilitators equipped to support delivery at community level.
The launch therefore represents a beginning rather than an endpoint. The longer-term goal is to embed effective violence-prevention approaches within national and local systems, supported by trained personnel, safeguarding and referral mechanisms, community engagement, monitoring and sustained government ownership.

item.title: One Girl Married Every Three Seconds as World Falls Behind on Promise to End Child Marriage
item.description:
Countries: World, Bangladesh, occupied Palestinian territory, Sierra Leone
Source: Save the Children

LONDON/GENEVA, 27 November 2026 – Nearly one girl every three seconds is married before the age of 18 despite world leaders committing more than 10 years ago to end child marriage by 2030, said Save the Children said on the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage[1] [2].

Save the Children said progress at ending child marriage has slowed to a crawl, leaving millions of girls at risk of being denied their childhoods, education, safety and future opportunities.

Global child marriage rates have fallen by just 3.4 percentage points since 2014, from 21.9% to 18.5%, and have barely shifted in the last two years [3]. At the current pace, the world is dangerously off track to meet its commitment to end child marriage in the next four years with hard-won gains at risk of reversal, said the child rights organisation.

The warning comes as conflict, climate shocks, displacement, economic pressures and shrinking international aid budgets push more families towards negative coping mechanisms including marrying off their daughters.

According to the Girls Not Brides network, of which Save the Children is a member, 12 million girls are married before the age of 18 each year – around 23 girls married every minute, or 1 girl married every 3 seconds.

In Gaza, latest UN data reveals a significant rise in early and forced marriages incidents, with a stark 123% increase between the first two quarters of 2026. While most reported incidents (67%) involved women aged 18- 59, girls aged 12-17 accounted for 16% of cases.

Despite the alarming slowdown in progress, Save the Children said countries that have invested consistently in girls’ rights and protection demonstrate that change is possible.

In Bangladesh, for example, while nearly half the country’s women aged 20 to 24 were married before age 18, of child marriage rates fell from 62.7% to 47.2% over roughly the same period that global progress stagnated [4]. This was due to no single initiative but sustained political commitment and targeted investments in social protection, girls' education, community-led norm change, prevention and response to gender-based violence, and initiatives that strengthened girls' agency and ability to exercise their rights.

Sierra Leone has also demonstrated how sustained advocacy and political commitment can drive progress. Recently, years of advocacy led by girls, communities, civil society organisations and development partners helped secure stronger legal protections for girls, including the adoption of the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2024. Since then, the 2026 “Never Before 18” campaign, supported by Save the Children, has helped maintain public and political attention on ending child marriage by elevating girls' voices, raising awareness of the law, and calling for its effective implementation across the country.

Rahinatu Adamu Hussaini, Save the Children’s Global Senior Advisor on gender-based violence prevention and response, said:

“Child marriage is not a cultural inevitability or a rite of passage It's a deadline imposed on a girl before she's had the chance to write her own story. It's both a harmful practice, and a form of gender-based violence that violates girls' rights to education, health, bodily autonomy and freedom from violence.

“Yet today, nearly one girl every three seconds is married before the age of 18, forced into a harmful practice that cuts short her childhood, limits her choices, and increases her risk of violence, poor health outcomes and lifelong inequality.

“That's why this new international day matters. It reminds us that behind every statistic is a girl whose rights, aspirations and future are at stake, at a time when progress is stalling and investment in proven solutions is under threat.

" The good news is that we know what works. Child marriage declines when governments invest in girls' education, strengthen social protection systems, prevent and respond to gender-based violence, and create opportunities for girls to participate in decisions that affect their lives.

"Countries such as Bangladesh have shown that progress is possible when commitments are matched with sustained investment and accountability. The challenge before us is not a lack of solutions; it is ensuring those solutions reach the girls who need them most."

Save the Children is urging governments, donors and international institutions to urgently step up funding for solutions that are proven to reduce child marriage, including education for girls, support for vulnerable families, protection from violence, and opportunities for girls to shape their own futures.

Every girl, everywhere, should be able to decide if, when and whom to marry, and to grow up free from violence, coercion and discrimination.

NOTES:

[1] According to the Girls Not Brides network, of which Save the Children is a member, 12 million girls are married before the age of 18 each year – around 23 girls married every minute, or 1 girl married every 3 seconds.

[2] On 4 September 2026, the United Nations General Assembly adopted resolution A/RES/80/309, proclaiming 27 November as the International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage. The resolution recognizes that these practices violate, abuse or impair human rights and disproportionately affect women and girls, particularly those in vulnerable situations. They can threaten access to education, health, economic opportunities and the full enjoyment of human rights.

[3] UNICEF Global Database on Child Marriage / Save the Children Child Atlas data on Child Marriage

[4] UNICEF Global Database on Child Marriage / Save the Children Child Atlas (According to UNICEF data, the proportion of women aged 20-24 in Bangladesh who were married before age 18 declined from 62.7% to 47.2%, demonstrating significant progress despite continued challenges. The latest estimate of 47.2% comes from the Bangladesh Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 2025.

item.title: World: Waiting to tackle HIV in the Pacific could double the cost and prevent fewer infections
item.description:
Countries: World, Fiji, Papua New Guinea
Source: Australian National University

Caroline van Gemert

Anna Bowring

Jason Mitchell

Donald Wilson

Across the Pacific, communities are confronting growing human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) outbreaks at a time when health budgets are constrained and international development assistance is increasingly uncertain. Fiji has one of the fastest-growing HIV epidemics globally, with new infections rising approximately twelvefold between 2010 and 2025. Papua New Guinea has declared a national HIV crisis, while several other Pacific Island countries and territories are now reporting early warning signs of increased transmission.

When responding to an HIV outbreak, when to invest, how much to invest and what to invest in all shape outcomes. The challenge is not only to secure enough funding, but to make sure it reaches the right people and arrives early enough to change the course of an outbreak.

To examine these trade-offs, we used Optima HIV, a mathematical and economic modelling tool that has been applied around the world to identify how HIV resources can be allocated to minimise new infections and HIV-related deaths.

We modelled a hypothetical Pacific Island country of 100,000 people with an emerging HIV outbreak, using regional epidemiological, behavioural, service and cost data. We compared current approaches with an optimised response: treatment and adherence support for people already diagnosed, plus targeted prevention and testing for key populations. Key populations are the groups most affected by HIV, such as men who have sex with men and people who inject drugs, and they often have limited access to services. We tested this response across several outbreak profiles, starting in either 2027 or 2030.

Four findings emerged: act early, prioritise treatment and adherence support for people already diagnosed, focus prevention and testing on key populations and expect costs to rise before they fall.

First, acting early costs less and prevents more infections. Doubling existing annual HIV investment from 2027 (from about USD32,700 to USD65,500 per 100,000 population per year) and optimising the response was projected to avert more than 90% of new infections by 2040, compared with continuing current approaches. Delaying this response until 2030 would cost on average USD132,500 per 100,000 population per year to achieve a similar result — about twice the annual cost of investing from 2027 — yet would avert fewer infections (86%).

The difference in effectiveness and cost between an early and a delayed response comes down to how HIV spreads. Transmission compounds over time, so an infection prevented today also prevents infections further along the chain. As an outbreak accelerates, a much larger investment is needed just to regain lost ground.

Second, maximising treatment engagement and outcomes among people who are diagnosed is the priority. In the model, scaling up treatment, engagement in care and adherence support did the most to increase viral suppression and prevent onward transmission. Fiji shows why this matters: only 56% of reported people living with HIV were receiving antiretroviral treatment at the end of 2025, and only 15% of those on treatment had documented viral suppression, meaning the virus had been reduced to a level that prevents onward transmission. Coverage across all people estimated to be living with HIV in Fiji, including those not yet diagnosed, is lower still: Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS puts it at about 22%.

Third, prevention and testing should focus first on key populations. Testing and prevention services designed for these groups had a bigger impact than generalised testing and condom programs, because this is where the virus spreads.

Fourth, spending rises first, then falls. Reported diagnoses reveal only part of an outbreak. In our model, around 31% of people living with HIV were diagnosed in 2025, so expanded testing finds many more people who need treatment and adherence support, and that raises costs in the short term. But as future infections are prevented, those projected needs decline. Within about a decade, an optimised response was projected to need fewer treatment and adherence resources than continuing with current approaches.

Together, the findings show countries do not need to wait to deliver a perfect HIV response. Where resources are limited, starting with the interventions most likely to interrupt transmission, then expanding as resources and capacity grow, is more effective than delaying action.

This is not an argument for less HIV funding in the Pacific. It is an argument for targeted investment. Additional domestic and development-partner investment is critical. The finding is that the timing of investment can be just as consequential as its size.

These findings are not a prescription for any individual Pacific country. Local epidemiology, service costs, practical constraints and equity priorities must shape how governments invest. Country-specific Optima models can be built using national epidemiological and program data, with local priorities in mind, and we would welcome the chance to work with ministries and partners to do so.

Which key populations to reach first depends on the outbreak, and in many Pacific countries it is not yet clear what is driving the rise in infections or which populations are affected. Transmission patterns differ between countries and change over time, so we modelled different outbreak profiles, including varying sexual and injecting drug-use-related risks. Without a clear picture of who is most affected, governments cannot be sure where to direct scarce resources. That is why better surveillance data matters: timely local data on who is being infected, and whether they are reaching care, is what allows countries to target their response and adjust it as the outbreak changes.

For governments and development partners, the priority should be to secure effective funding before transmission accelerates, to protect services that reach key populations, to support people to start and stay on treatment and to ensure programs can adapt to local needs. Sustained investment, strong surveillance, better case monitoring and sound epidemiological data are crucial to directing resources as outbreak patterns change.

Pacific governments have already signalled where they want to go. At the 17th Pacific Heads of Health meeting in Rarotonga in August 2026, heads of health accepted two recommendations.

The first is that every Pacific Island country and territory develop or strengthen a national HIV preparedness and response plan within 12 months, including functional HIV surveillance and real-time early-warning indicators. The second is that a Pacific HIV Regional Support Mechanism be established within 18 months. These measures provide a foundation for the kind of early, targeted and sustained investment supported by our modelling. The commitments have been agreed. What they need now is resourcing.

HIV transmission does not pause while budgets are negotiated. The cost of waiting is paid twice: in preventable infections today, and in the greater resources needed to control outbreaks tomorrow.
